did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jeremiah chapter 46 opens with a prophecy concerning the nations, centered on prophecies about Egypt and its army.
Did you know? The battle described at Carchemish is dated to the fourth year of Jehoiakim, king of Judah. In it, Pharaoh Necho’s army was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.

Did you know? The description of the army preparing for battle includes shields, bucklers, horses, cavalrymen, spears, and armor—military equipment that illustrates the strength of the Egyptian army before the battle.
Did you know? Egypt is compared to the rising and surging Nile, an image expressing its desire to flood the land, destroy cities, and subdue their inhabitants.
Did you know? Egypt’s army is also said to include auxiliary forces and archers from Cush, Put, and Lud. Thus, the army is portrayed as being composed of different groups.

Did you know? The day of battle by the Euphrates is described as a “day of vengeance” and as a sacrifice to the Lord, while the sword is portrayed as eating, being satisfied, and drinking its fill of the enemies’ blood.
Did you know? After Egypt’s defeat, its disgrace and cries are described as spreading among the nations, and the verse concludes: “Warrior stumbled against warrior; both fell together.”
Did you know? In the second part of the chapter, it is said that Nebuchadnezzar will come and strike the land of Egypt, in addition to the defeat already described at Carchemish.

Did you know? Egypt is compared to a “beautiful heifer,” but the enemy from the north is described as coming to strike it. Its mercenaries are also compared to calves from the stall that flee and do not stand their ground in battle.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, comfort is offered to Israel: it should not be afraid, because the Lord will save it from exile, restore it to tranquility, and not completely destroy it—even though He will discipline it justly.
